---
title: "AI in measurement: Facilitator's guide"
output: html_document
---

This guide is for the person running the one-day workshop "AI in
measurement" with the mirtverse R package. It goes with `slides.Rmd` in
the same folder. The day suits 8 to 30 participants who know item response
theory (IRT) and have used R, such as psychometricians, testing-program
staff and graduate students. No one needs to have trained a machine
learning model or used a language model before.

## Before the day

**Two weeks before.** Send participants these instructions:

```r
install.packages(c("mirt", "learnr", "remotes"))
remotes::install_github("okanbulut/mirtverse")
library(mirtverse)
run_lab("auto-scoring")   # should open a lab in the browser
```

Ask them to read the AI Hub page on the mirtverse site (ten minutes) and to
bring one AI use from their own work, planned or real.

**The day before.** Run each of Labs 7 to 10 to the end yourself, and keep
the answer key open (the "Teaching labs" article on the mirtverse site,
section "Answer key"). Render the slides with `rmarkdown::render("slides.Rmd")`.
Check that the room has power for every laptop. Nothing needs the
internet, but installing packages on the day does.

**Pairs.** Labs work best in pairs, one person typing. Mix people from
different programs or roles.

## The schedule

| Time | Session | What participants do |
|---|---|---|
| 9:00 to 9:45 | What changes and what does not | Slides; a two-minute round of the AI uses they brought |
| 9:45 to 11:00 | Automated scoring | Lab 7, `run_lab("auto-scoring")` |
| 11:00 to 11:15 | Break | |
| 11:15 to 12:30 | Item text and difficulty | Lab 8, `run_lab("item-text")` |
| 12:30 to 13:30 | Lunch | |
| 13:30 to 14:45 | Automatic item generation | Lab 9, `run_lab("aig")` |
| 14:45 to 15:00 | Break | |
| 15:00 to 16:15 | Auditing an AI-scored test | Lab 10, `run_lab("ai-audit")` |
| 16:15 to 17:00 | Governance, and what to do on Monday | Slides; each participant writes their Monday plan |

Each lab session is 75 minutes: Ten minutes of slides, 50 of lab work and
15 for discussion. If a lab runs long, cut its last section rather than the
discussion, which is where the day's ideas get connected.

**Half a day instead?** Keep the opening, Lab 7 and Lab 10, and the
governance session: Together they take an engine from training to audit.

## Session by session

### 1. What changes and what does not

**Goal.** Participants leave the session sure that their training applies:
AI changes how parts of a test are made, not what the scores must show.

**Say.** Start from the jobs in the room, not from the technology. Use the
translation slide to show that most machine learning words have a
measurement twin. Introduce the rule for the day: The model drafts,
something else checks, a person decides.

**Ask.** "What AI use did you bring, and who checks it now?" Write the uses
on a board and come back to them in the last session.

### 2. Automated scoring (Lab 7)

**Goal.** Participants can judge a scoring engine with QWK, SMD and PRMSE,
overall and within groups, and choose its role.

**Watch for.** People who judge the engine on the students it was trained
on; the lab splits by student for a reason. People who stop at a high QWK;
the problem is in the group SMD.

**Discuss.** "The engine agrees with raters as well as raters agree with
each other. Is that enough?" Bring out that raters can share a bias the
engine then learns.

### 3. Item text and difficulty (Lab 8)

**Goal.** Participants can predict difficulty from item text, judge the
prediction by cross-validation, and say what it can and cannot replace.

**Watch for.** The leaky feature: Its near-perfect prediction is the
point of the exercise. Hold back the answer until most pairs have found it.

**Discuss.** "When would you trust a predicted difficulty enough to skip a
field test?" Bring out the difference between a new item of a known kind
and a new kind of item.

### 4. Automatic item generation (Lab 9)

**Goal.** Participants can write and fix an item model, and check after a
field test whether its items are equally difficult.

**Watch for.** Pairs who stop after generating items: The lab's lesson is in
the calibration, where two families turn out not to be isomorphic for
different reasons.

**Discuss.** "Who reviews generated items, and how many?" Bring out that a
reviewed template is not a reviewed item.

### 5. Auditing an AI-scored test (Lab 10)

**Goal.** Participants can run an audit, separate differential scoring from
DIF and drift, and turn the results into a validity argument.

**Watch for.** Drift that pooling the two years hides, and the DIF that has
nothing to do with the engine. Both are planted; ask pairs to explain each
in one sentence.

**Discuss.** "Which scores can be reported this year, and what does the
technical advisory committee need to see?"

### 6. Governance, and what to do on Monday

**Goal.** Participants leave with a plan for one AI component of their own.

**Do.** Go back to the uses on the board. For two of them, ask the room:
Who owns it, what evidence exists, what is the next check? Then give
everyone ten minutes to write their own Monday plan from the last slide.

**Mention, briefly.** The experimental slide on language models as
respondents. Keep it short: The point is that a fluent answer is not a
measurement, the same point as the rest of the day.

## When something goes wrong

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| A lab does not open | Check `library(learnr)` loads; restart R; try `learnr::run_tutorial("auto-scoring", package = "mirtverse")`. |
| A lab exercise is slow | Some exercises fit IRT models; ask the pair to wait a minute, or show the result on your screen. |
| "Which model is this?" | None: The language-model answers are recordings, written to show typical behaviour and mistakes, so everyone sees the same result. |
| A participant wants a live model | After the day, `mv_ask_setup()` connects Claude, OpenAI or a local model through Ollama; `mv_llm_record()` saves a session to replay in class. |
| A pair finishes early | Ask them to build a lab on their own data with `new_lab()` and the AI sections (the instructor toolkit article on the mirtverse site), or to read a chapter's "Your turn". |

## After the day

Send the slides, the links to the AI Hub and the reading list, and a short
form with three questions: What will you do on Monday? What was least
clear? What should the next workshop cover?
